report.answer_text:
What was notable: A colossal squid was filmed in its natural environment for the first time since it was identified and named 100 years ago.[1] Before this, colossal squid had only been seen when fishermen caught them or brought them to the surface.[1] The animal was also a juvenile. It was nearly one foot long and had a see-through appearance.[1] Scientists hope to eventually film a fully grown adult. The footage gives researchers a starting point for studying the species, since its life history is poorly known.[2] Experts confirmed the identification partly from the unusual hook arrangement on its arms.[3]
Where and how: The team on Schmidt Ocean Institute's Research Vessel Falkor (too) filmed the 30-centimeter squid at a depth of 600 meters (1,968 feet). They used the remotely operated vehicle SuBastian on March 9, during an Ocean Census expedition searching for new marine life.[1] The expedition was in the remote South Sandwich Islands in the South Atlantic Ocean.[1]
Related find: The same institute also captured the first confirmed footage of the glacial glass squid, *Galiteuthis glacialis*, in the Bellingshausen Sea near Antarctica, during its January 2025 expedition.[4]
